I’ve open-sourced Agent Lint, a linter for configuration used by Codex and other coding agents:
https://github.com/zhupanov/agent-lint
It validates things including:
.codex/ and .codex-plugin/
AGENTS.md
.agents/skills/
MCP configuration
Claude Code configuration
Cursor configuration
The project currently has ~300 lint rules, with a documented rule registry.

items.title: Agent Lint: open-source linter for Codex, AGENTS.md, MCP, Claude Code, and Cursor config

items.snippet:
I build ghfs. It keeps a repository's GitHub issues on disk as Markdown files, mounted read-only at .ghfs/ in the repo, so a coding agent reads an issue with cat instead of calling GitHub in the middle of a task. Disclosure up front: it is a paid product and it is not open source. The free tier covers one repository; unlimited repositories are $5/month or $48/year.
The Codex-specific part is the sandbox. Codex CLI's default workspace-write sandbox runs with network access off, so gh issue view 4
items.title: ghfs: GitHub issues as read-only local files, readable from inside Codex's sandbox

items.snippet:
The problem
My AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files kept growing, but I had no safe way to tell which instructions were still useful and which were stale, duplicated, or too broad.
So I built Skill Sunset, a local, read-only audit for agent instruction files. The important constraint is: TEST is not RETIRE. A suspicious rule is not removed just because a heuristic dislikes it.
npx skill-sunset@latest audit --codex --open
It scans AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and generic SKILL.md files, then produces an eviden
items.title: Skill Sunset: a local, read-only audit for stale AGENTS.md rules

items.snippet:
Instructions files are advice. The agent reads them, agrees, and then writes the thing you told it not to — a hardcoded connection string, a duplicate route handler, await on a synchronous call.
Sarge makes the rules enforceable instead of advisory. Every file the agent writes gets judged against a rule book in the repo — by a local model, not a regex — and the run refuses while a rule is broken. The agent gets the failure back and fixes it. items.title: Sarge: a rule check that refuses the run, instead of another line in the instructions file

items.snippet:
I run a few projects with Codex and Claude Code, and the part that wore me out was not the coding. It was being the operator: opening terminals, making worktrees, checking which agent was stuck, reading their pull requests, answering the same permission prompts. So I built the operations layer and open-sourced it.
Agent 007 (https://github.com/bill10/agent-007) is a small web app, one command (npx @bill10/agent-007), that:

starts Codex (or Claude Code, or any CLI agent) in web terminals, each i
items.title: Agent 007: a job board and a manager agent for Codex (and Claude Code) workers, in your browser

I built a lightweight Codex plugin experiment around repository-local guidance maps:

The plugin generates and refreshes a compact AGENTS.md action map for a codebase. It focuses on information that future Codex sessions often need before editing:

module ownership
task routing
dependency boundaries
project-specific editing rules
key entry points for each module

I'm developing MAIOS Project Kernel, an open-source semantic operating kernel for AI agents. It keeps sources, intent, competences and consequences connected so the agent can maintain orientation as its work changes: understand what the situation calls for, form useful capacities and let what happens change how it continues.
